# 1 Samuel Chapter 11 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folio 166v–167r | **Source Image:** 1SA_011_page_001.jpg, 1SA_011_page_002.jpg

---

**1** Nahash the Ammonite marched up and laid siege to Jabesh-gilead. All the men of Jabesh said to Nahash, "Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you."

**2** But Nahash the Ammonite replied, "I will make a treaty with you on one condition: that I gouge out the right eye of every one of you and bring disgrace on all Israel."

**3** The elders of Jabesh said to him, "Give us seven days to send messengers throughout the territory of Israel. If no one comes to rescue us, we will surrender to you."

**4** When the messengers arrived at Gibeah of Saul and reported the terms to the people, everyone broke down and wept.

**5** Just then, Saul was coming in from the fields behind his oxen. He asked, "What is wrong with the people? Why are they crying?" They told him what the men of Jabesh had reported.

**6** When Saul heard their words, the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he burned with fierce anger.

**7** He took a pair of oxen, cut them into pieces, and sent the pieces throughout the whole territory of Israel by messengers who proclaimed, "This is what will be done to the oxen of anyone who does not march out behind Saul and behind Samuel!" A God-sent terror fell on the people, and they turned out as one man.

**8** When Saul mustered them at Bezek, the Israelites numbered three hundred thousand, and the men of Judah thirty thousand.

**9** They told the messengers who had come, "Say this to the men of Jabesh-gilead: 'Tomorrow, by the time the sun is hot, you will be rescued.'" When the messengers went back and reported this to the men of Jabesh, they were overjoyed.

**10** The men of Jabesh then told Nahash, "Tomorrow we will come out to you, and you may do to us whatever you see fit."

**11** The next morning Saul organized his forces into three divisions. They broke into the Ammonite camp during the last watch before dawn and slaughtered them until the heat of the day. The survivors were so thoroughly scattered that no two of them were left together.

**12** Then the people said to Samuel, "Who was it that said, 'Should Saul reign over us?' Hand those men over, and we will put them to death!"

**13** But Saul declared, "No one will be put to death today, because today the LORD has accomplished a great deliverance in Israel."

**14** Then Samuel said to the people, "Come, let us go to Gilgal and there reaffirm the kingship."

**15** So all the people went to Gilgal, and there, in the presence of the LORD, they made Saul king. They offered fellowship sacrifices before the LORD, and Saul and all the Israelites celebrated with great rejoicing.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 2 — "gouge out the right eye":** Nahash's demand to blind the right eye (נְקוֹר לָכֶם כָּל־עֵין יָמִין) is not random cruelty. The right eye was essential for combat — warriors held their shields on the left side, covering the left eye, and sighted with the right. Nahash is proposing to render Israel permanently unable to fight. The word חֶרְפָּה ("disgrace") reveals his true aim: not just submission, but national humiliation.

**Verse 6 — "the Spirit of God rushed upon him":** The Hebrew וַתִּצְלַח רוּחַ־אֱלֹהִים עַל־שָׁאוּל uses the same verb (צלח) as in Judges for the Spirit's empowering of Samson and others. The Spirit does not merely inspire — it invades, it seizes. Saul's anger is not human rage; it is divine fury channeled through a human vessel. This is the moment Saul fully becomes the king Israel needs.

**Verse 7 — Cutting up the oxen:** This brutal summons echoes the horrific event of Judges 19:29, where the Levite dismembered his concubine to rally the tribes. The parallel is intentional: Saul uses oxen instead of a human body, but the message is the same — national emergency demands total mobilization. The phrase פַּחַד יהוה ("the dread/terror of the LORD") confirms that this is no mere political maneuver but a Spirit-empowered call to arms.

**Verse 13 — "the LORD has accomplished a great deliverance":** Saul's finest moment. He deflects vengeance, credits God, and shows mercy to his opponents. The Hebrew כִּי־הַיּוֹם עָשָׂה יהוה תְּשׁוּעָה בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל is a confession of faith: it is God who saves, not the king. This magnanimity will make Saul's later descent into paranoia and vindictiveness all the more heartbreaking.

**Verse 14 — "reaffirm the kingship":** The Hebrew וּנְחַדֵּשׁ שָׁם הַמְּלוּכָה means literally "let us renew the kingship there." This is not a second coronation but a ratification — the doubters of 10:27 have been silenced by Saul's military triumph, and the nation now unites behind him. Gilgal, the site of Israel's first encampment in the Promised Land (Joshua 4–5), lends ancient sacred weight to the moment.

— PNEUMA
